extracted.intended_audience: readers, critics, and novelists interested in the craft of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on reading, analysing, and constructing novels: how to perceive a book's form, the uses of different narrative modes (scene, picture, panorama, point of view), and how critic and novelist share responsibility for making the book. Emphasises deliberate, constructive reading and technical understanding of narrative devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: A book has a form
rubrics_metrics.description: A book is a thing to which a shape is ascribable—an artistic form that can be good or bad; the novel is not merely episodes or characters but a completed, detached object ('the book itself').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the novel is experienced as a flowing procession of impressions, critics and readers must attempt to recreate the novel as a single, coherent form. The form is often elusive in memory and must be deliberately constructed by the reader. Examples: Tolstoy, War and Peace—vast panorama complicates neat composition but still has parts of lucidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aright / reconstruct the book
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning of criticism is to read aright: to get into touch with the book and to recreate the book in the reader's mind so that its form can be judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading 'creatively' or constructively means holding the novel at a distance, resisting being lost in its life, and assembling impressions into a stable image; otherwise the critic only recalls fragments (scenes/characters) and cannot judge the book's making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic as co-creator / reader must become a novelist
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical reader must actively create a book in his mind; the critic shares responsibility for making the book as an artistic whole because the author cannot implant the book entire into another's brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critic should not be merely receptive: he must marshal impressions into a structure, recognize varied 'substances' of the novel (forms of narrative), and produce an appraisable, coherent book in memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelist's selection and arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's primary work is selection and arrangement: lifting fragments from life, discarding the accidental, remaking them under conditions where they can express themselves and be distributed in a single design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic must accept the author's selection as authoritative and then work with that material to judge its disposition; the novelist's role is distinct but intersecting with the critic's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the different narrative modes
rubrics_metrics.description: There are various forms of narrative (dramatic, pictorial, scenic, generalized, panoramic, etc.), each with distinct properties and purposes in a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and writers must learn to discern these modes in order to use them properly; terms like 'dramatic' and 'pictorial' are metaphors but necessary for technical discussion. The book advocates studying masterworks to see how modes are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy and prudence of the dramatic scene
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic incident or scene is of first importance: it is the sharpest effect and should be used to clinch matters and deliver the final stroke where emphasis is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenes sparingly and prudently—do not squander dramatic presentation. A scene shows its whole time and space and is 'expensive' in narrative time; it should often be prepared by other means and used to crown an effect rather than to carry all the burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of picture/panorama (pictorial narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Picture or panoramic narrative handles long reaches of time and space and accumulates impression over breadth; it is preparatory and complementary to dramatic scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Picture travels over periods and expanses economically, building broad impressions that scenes can later render sharply. Recognize the appropriate places to use pictorial rendering where broad survey is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of narrative devices (scene vs narrative compression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes are vivid but costly in length and cannot foreshorten time/space; narrative/description can compress time and cover more ground economically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should pick the method appropriate to the material: use concise narrative to indicate distances/periods, and reserve dramatization for moments that demand full presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare a scene—avoid unprepared dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: A dramatic scene is weakened if it is not prepared in advance; an unprepared scene 'wastes a portion of its strength.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange prior narrative or pictorial material so the scene can deliver its effect swiftly and sharply. Scenes should 'clinch' matters already pending rather than attempt to establish groundwork on the spot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use point of view / consciousness to convert picture into drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Centering the story in somebody's consciousness can dramatize pictorial material: by passing the story through a constituted mind, the author interposes a presence that makes pictorial report more than a mere mirror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct pictorial reporting feels thin, present the material as filtered through a character's consciousness (the 'mirror' of the mind) to gain dramatic intensity and solidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain distance to perceive form (avoid treating novel as mere life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers tend to forget that a novel is an object of art and treat it as a piece of life; to perceive form one must hold it at a distance and think of the book as shaped art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reader is wholly lost in the novel's illusion, he cannot see its composition. Critical reading requires detachment sufficient to assemble a coherent form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the 'substances' of a novel (technical elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many different 'substances' (forms of narrative, types of scene, devices) go to the making of a novel; the critic must know their capacities to use them aright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study examples in which these elements appear to discern their properties and learn how to combine them in construction and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcome shyness in analysis—don't fear dissecting novels
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a cultural shyness about analysing novels (as if to take them to pieces were to destroy them); critics should not be inhibited by this scruple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysing the making of a novel is legitimate and necessary; the pleasure of understanding the craft can exceed the pleasure of illusion and does not destroy the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice constructive reading to retain the book
rubrics_metrics.description: To recreate a book durably the critic must read constructively—deliberately reconstructing the form rather than passively collecting impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate, repeated, technically aware reading will extend the surviving image of a book and permit more precise criticism than casual reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form matters but vitality can compensate
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel's good form is desirable but not always decisive; some novels badly constructed may still triumph through vivid life and invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when a book's 'life' overrides formal defects; criticism should account both for structure and for vivacity of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a technical vocabulary for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical vocabulary for novels is impoverished and unsettled; terms like 'dramatic', 'pictorial', 'scenic', 'generalized' need clearer acceptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should work toward a more precise nomenclature by careful study and repeated use of terms grounded in observed technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match narrative mode to the story's stages
rubrics_metrics.description: When a novelist has his subject and point of view, he still must choose how to handle development—whether scenically, pictorially, panoramically, or by mixed means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should have a working theory about the relative uses of modes and apply each where its peculiar strength is required; the critic should look for and judge these choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid squandering the scene—favor fully-wrought unified scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelists often squander dramatic methods by gratuitous dialogue or unearned scenes; a fully-wrought scene in which every part acts to advance the story is rare and valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to place and shape scenes so they gather issues together and show outcomes organically; Flaubert's Bovary is cited as exemplary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's choice of subject is the cardinal gift
rubrics_metrics.description: How a novelist finds his subject is a primary talent; until a subject is announced criticism and exhortation are largely misplaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the subject is chosen, criticism and craft concern themselves with handling, point of view, and technique; the critic should follow the author's logic from the subject outward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert method's disability into strength (use limitations creatively)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods have inherent disabilities (e.g., pictorial report can be thin), but by admitting and emphasizing them an author can convert limitation into effect (e.g., dramatizing the mind that reports the picture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept a method's nature and exploit it—e.g., present things as pictures within a mind so that the 'mirror' itself becomes a dramatic object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism must focus on 'how the book was made'
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of criticism in fiction is to fasten upon the question of making—the technical aspect—rather than reiterating authors' biographies or general praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should study the craft and processes—selection, arrangement, modes of rendering—because understanding how books are constructed enables meaningful criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative study across many novels is required for inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish rules about when to use each narrative means one must examine and compare many novels in detail; single examples are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly work across a wide corpus would allow inductive conclusions about relative properties of scene, picture, panoramic treatment, etc.; critics and writers should pursue such study.
